title: Hostbusters: constraining $H_0$ and binary formation channels through gravitational-wave host galaxy associations
authors: Madeline L. Cross-Parkin, Ignacio Magaña Hernandez, Antonella Palmese, Paul D. Lasky, Eric Thrane
abstract: Gravitational-wave dark sirens can be combined with galaxy catalogues to provide a measurement of the Hubble constant. This inference requires assigning each potential host galaxy a probability of hosting a merger, but the appropriate weighting is uncertain because the binary merger rate may trace different galaxy properties, such as stellar mass or star formation rate, depending on the underlying formation channel. We introduce a flexible framework in which the dark-siren population is described as a mixture of two host-weighting prescriptions, with the mixing fraction inferred jointly with $H_0$. These components may be interpreted as subpopulations associated with distinct binary-formation environments. Using simulated catalogues, we show that marginalising over uncertainty in the host-population mixture preserves unbiased constraints on $H_0$, while allowing the gravitational-wave data to constrain the relative contribution of the two host populations. In particular, an A#-like detector network with $\mathcal{O}(10^3)$ dark sirens may be able to exclude scenarios in which the host population traces only one of the two weighting prescriptions. Dark-siren analyses may therefore provide robust cosmological measurements and new information about how merging compact binaries trace the galaxy population.
comments: 9 pages, 2 figures, 1 table

figs.cap: Posterior corner plot for $H_{0}$ and the mixing fraction, $\xi$, for different scenarios. The true values of $H_{0},\xi$ are marked with dashed lines. The two-dimensional plot shows one- and two-sigma credible intervals.

The two host-weighting tracers introduced in Sec. II.4 are the percentile ranks of these quantities. Their rank correlation is only $0.02$, and this near-independence allows the mixing fraction $\xi$ to be constrained.

title: A high-Galactic-altitude scattering screen: scintillation from Globular Cluster pulsar M53A
authors: Qiuyi He, Xun Shi, Dejiang Yin, Di Li
abstract: While known interstellar scattering screens are largely confined to the Galactic disk, the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the deep Galactic halo have remained unexplored. Using observations from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectra of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A). Under the 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models considered here, the inferred scintillation screen distances are $12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8}$\,kpc, respectively. These model-dependent estimates correspond to Galactic heights of $12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7}$\,kpc, placing the candidate screen among the highest-altitude scattering structures inferred to date. The strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry suggests substantial electron-density inhomogeneity within the screen. We speculate that this screen is associated with small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble. These results support the presence of discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep within the Galactic halo, far beyond the regions where localized stellar feedback is typically concentrated, and highlight pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM.

title: Constraints on the Cosmic Expansion Rate Using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey and the Fifth Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog
authors: Sean Patrick MacBride, Isaac McMahon, Danny Laghi, David Sánchez-Cid, Felipe Andrade-Oliveira, Marcelle Soares-Santos, Maciej Bilicki, Sarah Ferraiuolo, Surhud More, Rachel Gray, Gergely Dálya
abstract: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide a calibration-free measure of distances, offering important input on the long-standing tension between early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant ($H_0$). In the absence of an electromagnetic counterpart, the dark siren method can be employed to statistically correlate a gravitational wave event's localization with a galaxy catalog of potential hosts. We present a measurement of the Hubble constant using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey Data Release 3 and the fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog. Applying the dark siren method to a large, photometrically heterogeneous footprint required revised catalog-construction choices: a faint apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r<20$) to control known photometric-redshift bias, a bright apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r>15.5$) to exclude saturated sources, implementation of an evolving luminosity function parameterization, and de-biasing survey regions based on survey depth and photometric redshift precision. With these choices applied to DELVE, we obtain $H_0= 67.4^{+13.0}_{-11.2}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ from dark sirens alone, and $H_0= 70.6^{+8.7}_{-7.0}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ when combined with the bright siren GW170817. We test other galaxy catalog configuration choices, and find subdominant influence from photometric band choice and luminosity function parameterization on the final $H_0$ posterior. Our results demonstrate that extending the dark siren method to wider-area, non-uniform galaxy surveys is feasible and provides additional constraining power on $H_0$ relative to the spectral siren method, opening the door for analyses with forthcoming galaxy catalogs from LSST, Euclid, and Roman.
comments: 9 Pages, 6 Figures, 2 Tables, Submitted to A&A

title: Gravity-mode main-sequence asteroseismology of 16 open clusters and associations
authors: Gang Li, Haotian Wang, Anuj Gautam, J. S. G. Mombarg, Simon J. Murphy, Mara Bernizzoni, Mingjie Jian, Saakshi Wadhwa, Dario J. Fritzewski, Facundo D. Moyano, Prasad Mani, Chenyuan Li, Timothy R. Bedding, Conny Aerts
abstract: Coeval stellar populations offer a unique advantage for studying stellar physics because their members share a common age and broadly similar initial chemical composition, allowing the free parameters in stellar models to be constrained more efficiently. Meanwhile, asteroseismology, through the study of pulsation modes that propagate through stellar interiors, provides powerful constraints on internal structure and the physical processes operating beneath stellar atmospheres. The combination of coeval-population studies and asteroseismology therefore provides an unparalleled laboratory for testing and improving stellar evolutionary and structural models. Using light curves from the Kepler and TESS space missions, together with membership constraints based on Gaia astrometry, we identify g-mode period-spacing patterns in dozens of early-type ($T_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 7000\,\mathrm{K}$) main-sequence stars across 16 stellar groups. From these patterns, we infer near-core rotation rates $f_\mathrm{rot}$ and measure the asymptotic spacing $\Pi_0$ of g modes, tracing both angular-momentum transport and the evolution of the convective stellar cores. Using our homogeneous set of g-mode stellar-group members spanning a wide range of ages, we show that near-core rotation in early-type stars decreases with stellar evolution. We compare our results with existing model predictions. Our $\Pi_0$ measurements still show discrepancies with current stellar models for reasons that remain unclear, as reported in several previous studies. We also report two g-mode pre-main-sequence pulsators and three pulsating blue stragglers. Our sample provides a useful basis for calibrating stellar models in future ensemble asteroseismic studies of coeval stellar populations.
comments: 26 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJS

title: Gravitational Instability of Cold Axion Dark Matter Beyond Minimal Coupling
authors: Bryan Cordero-Patino, Álvaro Duenas-Vidal, Jorge Segovia
abstract: Following recent observations of unexpectedly massive galaxies at high redshift by the James Webb Space Telescope, the revision of Dark Matter (DM) models --specifically regarding how DM couples to gravity-- has become a central topic in Cosmology. In this paper, we develop an axion model for Cold Dark Matter (CDM) with a non-minimal coupling to gravity. From this framework, we evaluate the gravitational instability in the hydrodynamic limit. Our results demonstrate how gravitational instabilities depend on the non-minimal coupling parameter, providing a novel tool for aligning with the high-redshift observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.
comments: 10 pages, 4 figures

title: Kinematic structure and age of a Scorpius--Centaurus subcomponent: implications for PDS 70 planetary system
authors: Arunima Arunima, Mike Ireland, Mark Krumholz
abstract: PDS~70, the only system with two directly imaged protoplanets embedded in their natal disk, is a benchmark for giant-planet formation theory. Interpreting the planetary luminosities requires a precise age for the host star, but the widely adopted isochronal age of $5.4\pm1.0$~Myr is substantially younger than ages inferred for the Upper Centaurus--Lupus (UCL) population with which it is associated. We address this discrepancy by determining a new kinematic age for PDS~70 using radial velocities for 405 candidate members of the Scorpius--Centaurus T subcomponent from the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) on the ANU 2.3~m telescope, reducing uncertainties by a factor of $\sim5.5$ compared to \textit{Gaia}. %We supplement these measurements with H$\alpha$ and lithium equivalent widths as youth diagnostics. We combine these with \textit{Gaia} DR3 astrometry in the \texttt{Chronostar} kinematic reconstruction framework to derive a posterior-weighted kinematic age of approximately $10$--$15$~Myr for all the T subcomponent stars, with a kinematic age of $\approx 12$--$16$~Myr for PDS 70, ruling out ages as young as the published isochronal estimate. At this kinematic age, PDS~70~\textit{b}'s (and to a lesser extent, PDS~70~\textit{c}'s) luminosity is incompatible with warm-start cooling tracks under current dynamical mass constraints. The most natural interpretation is that PDS~70~\textit{b} formed $\approx10.5$ Myr after its host star, and no less than $\approx7.7$ Myr after it.

title: A 36.34-day Sub-Neptune Candidate Transiting the Nearby K Dwarf TIC 402710280
authors: Rishit Vora
abstract: We report a transiting sub-Neptune candidate with a period of 36.34 days around TIC 402710280 (TYC 9041-03677-1), a K dwarf of TESS magnitude 9.24 at 66.8 pc that the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has observed only in full-frame images. Four transits, recorded between 2021 and 2026 in Sectors 39, 93, 100 and 102 and reduced by three independent pipelines, share a depth of $2092 \pm 47$ ppm and a duration of $5.27 \pm 0.05$ h. Two of them fall on consecutive cycles, and every shorter period predicts transits in covered data that are absent at $\geq 18.6\sigma$; the period is $P = 36.33986 \pm 0.00051$ d. A transit model gives $R_p/R_\star = 0.0421^{+0.0007}_{-0.0005}$ and a stellar density consistent with the host's. The candidate has a radius of $3.75 \pm 0.22 R_\oplus$ and an equilibrium temperature of $498 \pm 21$ K. Difference-image centroids place the signal $1.5'' \pm 1.3''$ from the target. The only catalogued star close enough to contribute, a background star $3.5''$ away, would have to host an eclipsing binary whose eclipse shape is disfavoured for any main-sequence pair ($\Delta\chi^2 \geq 142$). No secondary eclipse is detected, and TRICERATOPS gives a false-positive probability of $0.003 \pm 0.004$. No high-resolution imaging exists, so companions within about $1''$ are constrained only by Gaia astrometry. The mid-times scatter about a linear ephemeris by 21.8 min (rms). Quick-Look Pipeline light curves reproduce the 29-min excess in the interval between the two 2026 transits, so it does not arise in our photometry; we report the scatter without choosing between an instrumental and a dynamical origin. The light curve also contains a $407 \pm 26$ ppm signal with a period of 3.78 days whose source, the target or the background star, the present data cannot identify. We predict transit times, including one in TESS Sector 114 on 2027 February 19.

title: The Solar System through dust maps. Encounter statistics with interstellar gas
authors: E. Maconi, J. Alves, S. Hutschenreuter, S. Ratzenböck, M. Pantaleoni, C. Zucker, C. Levy, G. Edenhofer
abstract: During its orbit around the Milky Way, the Solar System crosses different environments, including dense ISM regions. These encounters increase dust influx, leave geological signatures, and affect the heliosphere. For the local ISM, we estimate crossing frequencies and durations, the fraction of time spent above gas density thresholds, and how Solar vertical motion and ISM stratification influence these statistics. We quantify gas influx and dust exposure. We use Gaia-based 3D dust maps of the Solar neighborhood, sampled by integrating the Solar System along its Galactic orbit while rigidly translating the maps. From the resulting density time series, encounter statistics and fluxes are derived. We find that the Solar System spends most of its time in low density environments, while crossings of dense gas become rarer with increasing density threshold. For nH>=1cm^-3, the crossing frequency is above 600Gyr^-1, whereas thresholds around 200cm^-3 are crossed once per Gyr. Individual crossings last tens of kyr and become shorter at higher density thresholds. The inferred durations soon become nearly constant, reflecting the finite spatial resolution of the maps. The Sun spends 18 to 47% of the sampled time above 1cm^-3, and 1 to 10% above 10cm^-3. The residence fraction can be reproduced by combining the vertical volume filling factor of gas with the fraction of time spent by the Sun at each height. Within the current vertical range sampled by the Sun, we find no clear enhancement of crossing statistics during midplane passages, suggesting that these do not necessarily lead to periodic perturbations of the Solar System. About 50% of the gas influx is contributed by gas with nH<=3-4cm^-3, and about 90% by gas with nH<=48cm^-3. Our results provide a first order, data driven estimate of ISM encounter statistics, gas influx, and dust exposure along the Solar System's Galactic orbit.

title: Late-time distance consistency and model-independent curvature inference with strong lensing, quasars, and galaxy clusters
authors: Jian Hu, Yi Liu, Jian Ping Hu, Zhongmu Li
abstract: We revisit a late-time, model-independent distance-consistency framework that combines strong gravitational lensing systems (SGLS), ultraviolet/X-ray quasars (QSOs), and 38 Sunyaev--Zel'dovich/X-ray galaxy-cluster angular-diameter distances. The analysis focuses on systematics rather than on presenting a competitive curvature measurement. Starting from the 158-system SGLS catalog, we exclude 30 systems that violate the lensing-geometric requirement $D_{A,ls}/D_{A,s}<1$ in the isothermal reference case $\gamma_{\rm lens}=2$, leaving a fixed 128-system SGLS parent sample for cross-matching with 1598 QSOs. A deterministic maximum-cardinality, minimum-mismatch one-to-one assignment yields 100 SGLS--QSO pairs at the nominal $\Delta d/d=5\%$ threshold. We propagate the measured X-ray flux uncertainties and the intrinsic QSO scatter, and, crucially, we include the full $38\times38$ covariance induced by using the same QSO distances in the kernel-smoothed cluster predictions. With $\Omega_K\sim\mathcal{U}[-10,10]$, the joint posterior is $\Omega_K=2.085^{+1.634}_{-1.103}$ (68\%; central 95\% interval $[0.269,6.028]$). We do not interpret the positive shift as evidence for an open Universe. \added{This positive posterior offset is driven by cross-probe calibration tensions, sample-assignment effects, and the cluster anchor; it cannot be attributed to the intrinsic spatial geometry of the Universe.} The SGLS+QSO data alone leave curvature essentially prior dominated, $\Omega_K=0.70^{+6.33}_{-7.12}$, whereas removing only the off-diagonal cluster covariance moves the posterior to $\Omega_K=5.21^{+2.46}_{-2.07}$. Thus the cluster anchor supplies most of the curvature constraining power and its covariance materially changes the posterior location.

title: Pulse Morphology and Spectral Study of LPT J1634+44 Using GMRT
authors: Ashish Kumar, Yogesh Maan, Ayushi Shrivastava, Banshi Lal
abstract: Long-period radio transients (LPTs) are a recently discovered class of Galactic coherent radio emitters characterized by rotation periods of minutes to hours and highly polarized radio pulses. Their nature remains uncertain, with proposed scenarios invoking isolated or binary systems containing neutron stars (NSs) or white dwarfs (WDs). We investigate the nature of CHIME/ILT J1634+44 through multi-band observations with the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT), examining its pulse morphology, spectral evolution, and timing behavior. The pulses show substantial profile variability, and the subpulse features evolve significantly across observing frequencies. Using our measurements of quasi-periodic microstructures in J1634+44 pulses as well as those of other LPTs available from literature, we show that the scaling relationship between the rotation and microstructure periods is not limited to only neutron stars but extend to white dwarfs as well. The radio spectrum of J1634+44 is highly variable and exhibits a spectral turnover that shifts toward lower frequencies across observing epochs. Interpreting this turnover as free-free absorption, we constrain the physical properties of the intervening absorbing medium. Complementing these emission diagnostics, we also present analysis of pulse arrival times spanning approximately a decade to probe the previously proposed spin-orbit resonance models for this LPT.
comments: 18 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ, comments are welcome

title: Probing the Interstellar Medium towards the Double Pulsar and the Gum Nebula using Low-Frequency Pulse Broadening Measurements
authors: C. P. Lee, N. D. R. Bhat, B. W. Meyers, W. van Straten
abstract: Long-term timing of the double pulsar system (PSR J0737-3039A/B) has enabled some of the most stringent constraints on strong-field gravity. Yet, despite the system's high profile, there have been very few observations at frequencies below 300 MHz, where pulse broadening due to interstellar scattering becomes significant. Measurements of the pulse broadening timescale and its frequency scaling, $\tau_\mathrm{s}\propto\nu^\alpha$ (where $\alpha$ is the scattering spectral index), provide valuable constraints on the structure of the scattering medium. Here we report on simultaneous observations of J0737-3039A and five other nearby pulsars (J0630-3824, J0742-2822, J0820-4114, J0835-4510, J0837-4135) in the frequency range 109-231 MHz using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). These observations have enabled the highest-quality detections ever published for these pulsars at low frequencies. For J0737-3039A, J0742-2822, and J0837-4135, we measure $\alpha$ to be -4.1(1), -3.8(1), and -4.1(1), respectively. These measurements provide new constraints on the density and turbulence parameters of the Gum Nebula region, and we discuss implications for models of the Galactic electron density distribution. Our current data yield a dispersion measure (DM) precision of ~4 x 10^-4 pc/cm^-3 for J0737-3039A, which can be further improved with the MWA Phase III to reach ~1 x 10^-4 pc/cm^-3, far exceeding the precision of previous studies. The prospects for precisely constraining temporal variations in the DM and pulse broadening timescale strengthen the importance of regular monitoring of J0737-3039A at low frequencies, with the eventual goal of contributing to long-term timing studies.
comments: 22 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ

title: Effect of galaxy mergers on dust masses
authors: W. J. Pearson, M. Romano, K. Małek, D. Donevski, K. Lisiecki, A. P. Cotter, S. Dey, T. Goto, S. C.-C. Ho, D. J. Santos
abstract: Dust mass (M$_{Dust}$) is one of the key physical properties of galaxies that track the cold interstellar medium. However, the M$_{Dust}$ in merging galaxies is poorly understood. We aim to derive how the cold dust mass of galaxies is affected by major mergers at low redshifts. M$_{Dust}$ was estimated for approximately 500 major mergers in the North Ecliptic Pole extragalactic field using spectral energy distribution fitting runs with CIGALE, with different dust attenuation and emission models. We also analysed over 12 000 mergers from the SIMBA simulation using its M$_{Dust}$. We matched merging and non-merging systems in stellar mass, redshift, and local density, to enable a comparison of M$_{Dust}$. We then performed a second comparison using a control sample also matched in SFR. AGN host galaxies were then removed, and this matching repeated. Observed mergers have larger M$_{Dust}$ than the non-mergers by up to a factor of 1.82$\pm$0.35, or 1.60$\pm$0.44 without AGN-hosts. When matched by SFR, observed mergers show no significant change in M$_{Dust}$, both when including and excluding AGN-hosts. SIMBA galaxies show similar trends when AGN-hosts are included but there is still an increase in M$_{Dust}$ when matched by SFR. When AGN-hosts are excluded, the SIMBA mergers show smaller M$_{Dust}$ by a factor of 0.98$\pm$0.03, or 0.97$\pm$0.02 when matched in SFR. The higher the mass of a merger, the greater M$_{Dust}$ increase for observations for two of the CIGALE runs, or the smaller the decrease for SIMBA. Observed mergers are typically more dusty than their non-merging counterparts but only because they typically have higher SFRs, regardless of whether they host AGN or not. SIMBA mergers follow observations when AGN hosts are included, but show reduced M$_{Dust}$ when AGN hosts are removed. M$_{Dust}$ in SIMBA is linked to AGN in a way not seen in observations.
comments: 17 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, 3 appendices, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Competitive roles of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in isolated molecular cloud cores
authors: Daisuke Takaishi, Yusuke Tsukamoto, Miyu Kido, Shigehisa Takakuwa, Yoshiaki Misugi, Yuki Kudoh, Yasushi Suto
abstract: We investigate the impact of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in the gravitational collapse of isolated low-mass cloud cores using three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics simulations. In the models explored in this study, we find that unipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with the super-Alfvénic turbulence of $M_{\rm{A}}>1$, where $M_{\rm{A}}$ is the Alfvén Mach number of the initial cloud core. In contrast, bipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with $M_{\rm{A}}\lesssim1$. Our results suggest that the relative strength of the turbulence to the magnetic field in the initial cloud core plays a key role in the formation of unipolar outflows. We also find that no outflow is formed in cloud cores with the strong magnetic field of the dimensionless mass-to-flux ratio $\mu=2$. The outflow morphologies can be used as tracers to indirectly estimate the relative strengths of the turbulence and magnetic field of the parent cloud cores.
comments: Accepted for publication in PASJ

title: Disc breaking and parametric instability in warped accretion discs driven by differential precession
authors: Loren E. Held, Gordon I. Ogilvie
abstract: We present the first local simulations of accretion disc breaking (or disc tearing) with differential precession. Precession can occur due to a non-spherical potential (e.g. tilted circumbinary discs), or relativistic effects (e.g. tilted discs around spinning black holes). This tends to induce a twist in the disc, potentially causing it to break into rings. We extend earlier work on free (unforced) warps in Held+2026 [arXiv:2511.18655v1] to include differential precession in the shearing box, and carry out quasi-2D, isothermal, high-resolution ($N = 32$ cells per scale-height $H$) numerical simulations in which an imposed precession drives a warp in a tilted disc in either the wavelike ($\alpha < H/r$) or diffusive ($\alpha > H/r$) regime. Our key finding is that, at sufficiently large tilts and precession amplitudes, the disc breaks into multiple (4-5) mutually tilted rings exhibiting a rich morphology: from wide ($\sim 10H$), flat rings to compact tori of width $\sim H$. Interactions between rings occur as a result of oblique shocks that form in the gaps between them, leading to instances of disc rejoining. Smaller tilts and precession amplitudes lead instead to parametric instability of inertial waves in the disc. We develop a linear viscous theory of bending waves under the influence of an imposed precession. Finally, we present a systematic study of the effects of grid-based dissipation on tilted discs, and find that numerical dissipation damps the tilt and induces precession. This effect decreases with resolution as $\propto (1/N)^\beta$, $2.3 \lesssim \beta \lesssim 3.9$.
comments: Submitted to MNRAS

figs.cap: Top panel: radial profile of the oscillatory part of the vertical gravitational acceleration $g_{z}=-\Omega^{2}_{0}z[1+f(x)]$ (in units of $H_{0}\Omega_{0}^{2})$, where $f(x)=b\cos{kx}$ (see equation 6) at $z=H_{0}$ for a precession amplitude of $a=0.05$. (We have taken nodal and apsidal precession to be equal and opposite such that $b=a$.) The right-hand axis shows the corresponding radial profile of the nodal precession frequency in units of $\Omega_{0}$, $\omega_{\text{n}}(x)/\Omega_{0}=-(f/2)$. The remaining panels show radial profiles of the theoretical value of the real (in red) and imaginary (in blue) components of the complex tilt $Z=A\exp[\mathrm{i}\omega_{\text{n}}(x)t]$ that would develop in the absence of gas pressure, and of their radial derivatives, at two different times: $t=2.009\pi\Omega_{0}^{-1}$ (orbit 1) and $t=9.689\pi\Omega_{0}^{-1}$ (orbit 4.8). The initial amplitude (tilt) was taken to be $A=14H_{0}$. The dashed vertical lines mark the locations where the imposed precession is zero.

Evolution of a tilted disc (in the wavelike regime) under the influence of an imposed differential precession. The figures show density snapshots in the $xz$-plane from our fiducial simulation (Precession02) with a large initial tilt ($z_{0}=28H_{0}$) and precession amplitude ($a=0.05$). Top-left: the initial condition (orbit 0) is a flat, tilted disc. Top-middle (orbit 0.8): the imposed precession induces a warp in the disc. Top-right (orbit 3): horizontal sloshing motions in the disc converge into shocks at certain locations (magnified in the inset). Bottom-left: by orbit 33 the disc has broken into three rings. Bottom-middle (orbit 64): the disc begins to break into two more rings. We have labelled the different rings as A, B, C, D, and E, respectively. Bottom-right (orbit 100): the disc has broken into five rings (the two rings at the radial boundaries are actually the same ring). Three of the rings have lost most of their tilt and appear to be ‘rejoining’ again (at $x\sim\pm 35H_{0}$). There are two highly compact, tilted, and well-separated disc segments resembling tori at $x\sim-10H_{0}$ and $x\sim 5H_{0}$.

Time-evolution of volume-averaged radial (blue solid curve) and vertical kinetic energy density (black dot-dashed curve) taken from our fiducial simulation run with an initial disc tilt of $z_{0}=28H_{0}$ and a precession amplitude of $a=0.05$. Vertical dashed lines mark the times of the snapshots shown in Fig. 3.

Orbit-averaged radial profiles from our fiducial simulation (Precession02) with a large initial tilt ($z_{0}=28H_{0}$) and a large precession amplitude ($a=0.05$). See Section 2.3 for definitions. The orbit-average was taken over the first orbit (orbit 0-1). Top-left: warp amplitude $\langle\psi\rangle_{\tau}$. Top-middle: shear amplitude ($x$-component) $\langle U_{x}\rangle_{\tau}$. Top-right: surface density $\langle\Sigma\rangle_{\tau}$. Bottom-left: torque $\langle G\rangle_{\tau}$. Bottom-middle: shear amplitude ($y$-component) $\langle U_{y}\rangle_{\tau}$. Bottom-right: $xy$-component of the Reynolds stress $\langle R_{xy}\rangle_{\tau}$. The shaded areas show the approximate regions (in the left-hand part of the disc, only) at which gaps will open later on. The vertical dotted red line at $x=-22.5H_{0}$ shows the location (in the left-hand part of the disc) at which the imposed precession is zero. This is also the location at which the rate of change of precession is greatest. The dashed horizontal black line in the surface density plot shows the initial surface density.

Same as Fig. 5, but the radial profiles have been orbit-averaged over orbit 99–100. At this point the disc has broken into five rings (cf. bottom right-hand panel of Fig. 3). Two, compact Gaussian-shaped tori, C and D, straddle the centre of the domain and are separated by a deep gap. Further out, we have two wider rings, B and D, which are in the process of rejoining with the outermost ring (A).

Orbit-averaged tilt $Z$ in the complex plane for the broken disc segments C ("left-ring"; red) and D ("right-ring"; blue) from the fiducial simulation (see Fig. 3). Each data point is separated by a time-interval of one orbit. By orbit 125 the two rings are nearly out-of-phase, indicating that they are precessing independently.

title: Kinematics and Thermodynamics of Coronal Mass Ejections
authors: Soumyaranjan Khuntia
abstract: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are major drivers of space weather, yet their thermodynamic evolution remains insufficiently constrained. This thesis develops a comprehensive framework linking CME kinematics, thermodynamics, internal force balance, and geoeffectiveness through analytical modelling and multi-viewpoint observations. The developed FRIS model uses observed kinematics to infer otherwise inaccessible internal plasma properties, including the polytropic index. A systematic investigation of fast CMEs reveals an initial heat-release phase followed by a transition towards near-isothermal evolution, typically around 3-9 solar radii. The evolving contributions of thermal-pressure and centrifugal forces, opposed by the Lorentz force, establish a connection between expansion and thermal evolution. The findings demonstrate the limitations of assuming a fixed polytropic index in magnetohydrodynamic models of CME propagation. At 1 au, in situ observations reveal persistent non-adiabatic evolution, accompanied by turbulence and localised intermittency. The interacting CMEs associated with the May 2024 great storm show restructured magnetic and thermal configurations, producing double-flux-rope-like signatures and species-dependent heating, with electron thermodynamics as a better indicator of recent interactions. Statistical analysis of nearly 600 ME demonstrates that 45% exhibit net heating with a solar cycle dependence. Notably, High-impact ejecta preferentially exhibit stronger heating signatures, establishing thermal state as a complementary diagnostic of geoeffectiveness. Overall, this thesis establishes CMEs as intrinsically non-adiabatic systems whose thermodynamic evolution is coupled to expansion, internal force balance, solar-cycle variability, and CME-CME interactions, with important implications for understanding geoeffectiveness and improving space-weather assessment.
comments: PhD Thesis, Indian Institute of Astrophysics & Pondicherry University, 271 pages, Contributing papers have been published independently in ApJ, A&A, MNRAS and JAA journals

title: Linear Polarimetry of the Solar Corona during the Total Solar Eclipse of 8 April 2024: Multi-Band Observations and HDR Imaging
authors: Suprit Singh, Paras Sharma, Bharti Arora, Shivam Burman, Chaitanya Gandhi
abstract: High-Dynamic-Range (HDR) multi-band linear polarimetry of the solar corona during total solar eclipses provides a vital ground-based diagnostic tool for mapping plasma morphology and magnetic topology in the inner and middle corona. Extracting reliable polarimetric signals requires rigorous observational calibration, spatial co-alignment, and noise reduction via stacking. We report optical linear polarimetric observations acquired during the 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse from Dallas, Texas, USA, near solar maximum. Using a full-frame color CMOS detector paired with an 80~mm refractor, multi-band Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) images were recorded simultaneously across three polarizer orientations ($-60^\circ$, $0^\circ$, and $+60^\circ$) using a 9-step exposure bracket ($1/800\text{~s}$ to $1/3\text{~s}$). We present an end-to-end data-reduction pipeline incorporating: (i)~a novel astrometric registration framework that reconstructs Sun-centric solar-disk coordinates via lunar-limb fitting, catalog star plate-solving, and ephemeris displacement calculations, achieving sub-pixel alignment; (ii)~a photometrically linear exposure-normalization HDR image synthesis; and (iii)~Multi-scale Gaussian Normalization (MGN) coupled with Polarization-to-RGB chromatic mapping. The resulting structurally enhanced polarization composites unravel a complex solar-maximum coronal topology characterized by helmet streamers and fine-scale striations traceable out to $\sim3\,R_\odot$. This framework establishes a high-resolution, photometrically calibrated dataset ready for subsequent polarized brightness ($pB$) and electron density inversions.
comments: 23 pages, 8 figures. Accepted in Solar Physics

figs.cap: The figure shows the path of totality the April 8, 2024 total solar eclipse over the contiguous United States. The distinct line running directly through the middle of the purple/red band marks the centerline of the eclipse. Observers located exactly on this line experienced the maximum possible duration of darkness (totality). Stepping away from the central line reduces the the duration of the eclipse. The width of the band represents the physical diameter of the Moon’s darkest shadow (the umbra) as it projects diagonally onto Earth’s curved surface. Observers outside the band experience a partial solar eclipse. Our azimuth circle is shown centered on the data collection site in Dallas, Texas during totality (13:42:00 CDT). The dark yellow line towards the East points gives the azimuth of Sunrise, and the orange line towards the west gives the azimuth of Sunset, and the position of the Sun (orange circle) corresponds to its azimuth (slightly past the meridian) at the maximum totality, and the yellow arc denotes the Sun’s trajectory across the sky on the day of the eclipse. title: Linear gas mass density: a unifying descriptor of Cosmic Filaments
authors: Daniela Galárraga-Espinosa, Daisuke Nagai, Isabel Medlock, Mathieu Langer, Nabila Aghanim, Kentaro Nagamine
abstract: Cosmic filaments connect the nodes of the large-scale web and are thought to harbour a substantial fraction of the low-z baryon budget, yet a physically motivated framework for organising their diverse gas properties has been lacking. Here we show that the linear mass density $\Lambda$ = M_gas/L_fil, measured within the entropy radius r_K (the peak of the radial gas entropy profile) plays this role, analogous to mass in halo physics. Using TNG300-1 at z=0, we characterise the structural, thermodynamic, and chemical properties of 5637 filaments spanning more than two decades in $\Lambda$. Filaments form a continuous thermodynamic sequence with $\Lambda$, ranging from long, thin, cool, metal-poor structures to shorter, wider, hotter, and more enriched ones, with core temperatures spanning two orders of magnitude across the full WHIM window. The ratio of mass- to volume-weighted temperature reveals a shift in heat distribution: low-$\Lambda$ filaments have their hotter gas preferentially associated with denser material, whereas in high-$\Lambda$ filaments the hotter gas is diffuse. Well-defined scaling relations connect $\Lambda$ to temperature, electron density, pressure, entropy, and metallicity, with the T-$\Lambda$ scaling qualitatively consistent with gravitational heating. We present the first measurement of the gaseous linear mass density function, revealing a broad distribution with a flat low-$\Lambda$ regime and a steep exponential decline at high $\Lambda$, analogous to the halo mass function. The integrated Compton-y parameter $Y^{\rm int}$ scales systematically with $\Lambda$, providing a tSZ proxy accessible to current surveys. Finally, galaxy richness per unit length correlates tightly with $\Lambda$ (Pearson r=0.80), enabling $\Lambda$-based classification of filaments from spectroscopic surveys alone and guiding targeted searches for the missing baryons in the cosmic web.
comments: Comments are welcome!

figs.cap: Top: Gas entropy map in a thin slice of TNG300-1 at $z=0$. White dots mark $M_{*}>10^{9}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ galaxies used to trace the filament network with DisPerSE. Entropy gradients delineate the cosmic web, with filamentary structures visible as elongated regions of higher entropy compared to the background. Bottom: Zoom into two representative regions, with DisPerSE spines overlaid as black lines. The entropy increases from the inner to the outer parts of the filaments, producing a high-entropy boundary around the spine. This feature motivates the definition of $r_{K}$ as the radius of the entropy maximum (Sect. 3.2).

The green dashed-dotted distribution corresponds to the $r_{2}$ radii, with mean value 2.04 Mpc, discussed in Sect. 3.3 and shown here for comparison. The tails of the $r_{K}$ distribution reflect the physical diversity of the filament population: filaments with $r_{K}\lesssim 0.5$ Mpc are predominantly low-$\Lambda$ structures in underdense environments, while those with $r_{K}\gtrsim 3.5$ Mpc are high-$\Lambda$ filaments in denser large-scale environments near massive nodes (this is explored quantitatively in Sect. 4.1).

title: The Central Molecular Zone of our Galaxy, a chemical complexity factory: first interstellar detections of molecules towards G+0.693
authors: Víctor M. Rivilla
abstract: The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of our Galaxy is a prime laboratory for interstellar chemistry because of its extreme conditions, such as shocks and high cosmic-ray ionisation rates. It is an efficient factory of molecules, with many species first discovered in CMZ sources. This document reviews key results from the study of the CMZ G+0.693-0.027 molecular cloud. Using ultra-sensitive broadband spectral surveys together with laboratory spectroscopy, more than 140 molecules have been identified, including 28 detected for the first time in the interstellar medium (ISM). These discoveries include prebiotic precursors of biomolecules, increasingly complex members of known molecular families, molecules containing periodic third-row elements (S, P, Na, Mg), high-energy stereo- and structural isomers, and new cations. Overall, these findings extend the known limits of interstellar chemical complexity and highlight the CMZ's potential to provide the molecular ingredients for prebiotic chemistry.
comments: Part of "Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 405", M. Zajaček, T. Jerábková, V. Karas, R. Schödel & P. Suková, eds

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. I. Evidence from Low-angular-momentum, High-$α$ Stars Scattered Out of the Protodisk by Merger Events
authors: Tiancheng Sun, Maosheng Xiang, Shaolan Bi, Jifeng Liu, Meng Zhang, Yaqian Wu
abstract: Stars born in the high-$\alpha$ disk can later acquire low angular momentum through dynamical scattering during early merger events. Their age--metallicity distribution thus provides a fossil record of the history of both star formation and dynamical perturbations in the early Milky Way disk. Here we identify a sample of 2,078 such stars from more than two million Gaia DR3 subgiants with robust determinations of ages, kinematics, and abundances. From this sample we reconstruct their intrinsic age--metallicity distribution with a forward modeling approach. Our results confirm that these scattered stars are older and more metal-poor than the bulk of the high-$\alpha$ disk on average. In particular, the joint age--metallicity distribution reveals a robust two-component feature: a broad, dominant component with a peak age of $\sim$11.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.59$, and an older and more metal-poor component with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.86$. The presence of this two-component structure suggests that the high-$\alpha$ disk experienced episodic phases of star formation and chemical enrichment. The age distribution of the younger Splash component, compared with that of the high-$\alpha$ disk, provides evidence for a substantial dynamical perturbation at a lookback time of 10.8--11.5~Gyr, possibly associated with an early passage of Gaia--Sausage--Enceladus (GSE). The older Splash component, with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr, may preserve signatures of an earlier interaction, possibly associated with the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles (LKH) event.
comments: 19 pages, 10 figures, Published in AJ

title: Star formation history of Draco revealed by DESI DR1: suppressed early star formation efficiency for Milky Way dwarf galaxies
authors: Yujiao Yang, Maosheng Xiang, Yang Huang, Meng Zhang, Lanya Mou, Chao Liu, Jifeng Liu
abstract: Dwarf galaxies serve as fossils for understanding the early star formation history of the local Universe. In this work, we use stellar abundances for individual stars derived from the first data release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1) to investigate the star formation history of the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Draco. We simultaneously fit the stellar metallicity distribution function (MDF) and the [Mg/Fe]-[Fe/H] trend using the galactic chemical evolution (GCE) model flexCE. Our best-fit models imply a low star formation efficiency (SFE) of $0.003$ to $0.007\,\mathrm{Gyr}^{-1}$, which is about ten times lower than values reported in the literature, but consistent with recent SFE estimates for ultra-faint dwarf galaxies. By combining recent literature measurements, we find that the SFEs of Milky Way dwarf galaxies scale with stellar mass as $\mathrm{SFE}\propto M_\star^{0.24}$. A low star formation efficiency is associated with a strong outflow efficiency; we estimate a large wind mass-loading factor $\eta_{\mathrm{wind}}$ of approximately 172-260. This is well in line with the observed outflow-stellar mass relation and with the Feedback in Realistic Environment (FIRE) cosmological simulations. Our results demonstrate the power of large-scale, low-to-medium resolution stellar spectroscopic surveys to deliver robust constraints on the early formation history of galaxies in the local Universe.
comments: 19 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ

title: The accretion flow and jet of M87: broadband modelling across spatial scales
authors: Eduardo M. Gutiérrez, Santiago del Palacio, Tomás Tobías Mazzei
abstract: The nearby radio galaxy M87 is an ideal laboratory for studying accretion flows and relativistic jet emission. The EHT collaboration conducted the most comprehensive multi-wavelength observational campaign of M87, in which radio instruments with resolutions ranging from tens of microarcseconds to about an arcsecond sampled different portions of the outflow. We model these data using a radiatively inefficient accretion flow (RIAF) with winds and a new multi-zone jet model, initially magnetically dominated, in which we solve the transport equation for the non-thermal electrons as they are injected, advected, and cooled along the jet. We then compare each radio flux with the jet emission within an effective aperture set by the angular scale of the corresponding observation. The comparison across spatial scales favours a scenario in which the RIAF, rather than the jet, produces the compact $230~{\rm GHz}$ emission, while the jet dominates the lower-frequency radio, optical/UV and X-ray emission, but cannot produce the observed $\gamma$-rays. The RIAF connects the Bondi-scale gas supply to an accretion rate at the horizon of $1.1\times 10^{-5}$ of the Eddington rate, consistent with EHT polarimetry, and the two jets carry about a quarter of the accretion power, $1.2\times10^{43}~{\rm erg~s}^{-1}$ each. The framework presented in this work provides a simple way to disentangle the accretion-flow and jet contributions to the emission from nearby radio galaxies.
comments: 15 pages, 7 figures, submitted to journal

title: Joint Fit of Galaxy Cluster Scaling Relations from Individual Weak Lensing Data: Comparison with Stacked Analysis and a Real Data Test
authors: André Z. Vitorelli, Eduardo S. Cypriano
abstract: Stacking is the standard route to signal-to-noise in cluster weak lensing, but it destroys the cluster-by-cluster information that scaling-relation studies need. We instead fit every cluster's individual $\Delta\Sigma$ profile simultaneously, tying its mass and concentration to its own richness, redshift and magnitude gap, and compare with two stacked analyses of the same data: a forward-modelled stack sharing the same model and priors, and the standard two-step analysis. The magnitude gap (the BCG-to-brightest-satellite magnitude difference) enters the concentration, which the fossil-group picture ties to earlier assembly and more relaxed systems. On mock populations with triaxial haloes and miscentering, at DES Y3-like and LSST-like density, all three analyses recover the injected gap slope $\gamma_{\mathrm{cm}}$ with uncertainties that match the scatter between realisations, but not equally precisely: the joint fit scatters 1.2--1.3 times less than the forward-modelled stack, and 2 (DES-like) to 6.5 (LSST-like) times less than the two-step analysis, which is also biased in several other scaling-relation parameters. Applied to WaZP clusters with DES Y3 shears, the joint and forward-modelled fits agree on the gap coupling once the mass at fixed richness also depends on the gap, $\gamma_{\mathrm{cm}} = 0.065 \pm 0.033$ (forward-modelled) and$0.007^{+0.032}_{-0.033}$~mag$^{-1}$ (joint); the joint value is consistent with no coupling, so neither is a detection. The mass--concentration slope is consistent with zero in both, as expected from the upturn of the \citet{diemer2019} relation over this mass range. A gap coupling obtained in a model where the gap enters only the concentration need not survive a modest extension of that model.

title: Exploring the Evidence for Evolving Dark Energy with the Jeffreys prior
authors: Joshua Layton, Alex Hall, Naomi Clare Robertson
abstract: We investigate the impact of applying the uninformative Jeffreys prior in a re-analysis of DESI DR2 BAO, Planck 2018 CMB, and Type Ia Supernovae (DES-SN5YR, DES-Dovekie, Pantheon+, Union3). We incorporate this prior into new posterior inference and evidence calculations. We introduce novel techniques for interpreting the Jeffreys prior physically. To overcome the computational expense of the Jeffreys prior, we develop a fully $\texttt{JAX}$-based pipeline consisting of $\texttt{CosmoPower-JAX}$ emulators, gradient-based posterior inference using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), and evidence calculations using $\texttt{JAX}$-accelerated nested sampling. We demonstrate that while the parameter constraints on $w_0$ and $w_a$ remain robust to prior choice (exhibiting only minor shifts of the marginalised posterior towards the $\textit{Maximum A Posteriori}$ in less constraining dataset combinations), the Bayesian evidence is highly sensitive to the use of the Jeffreys prior; replacing uniform priors with the Jeffreys prior reverses the model-selection preference in dataset combinations that favour dynamical dark energy under the uniform prior, while strengthening existing preferences for $\Lambda$CDM. This is driven primarily by the significantly larger Occam penalty applied by the Jeffreys prior which penalises the overfitting of the data by a $w_0w_a$CDM model.

title: PRISMS/U13151. A Glimpse into the Earliest Phases of Galaxy Formation through an Ultra-Faint System $\approx$ 500 Myr after the Big Bang
authors: Pierluigi Rinaldi, Javier Álvarez-Márquez, Alejandro Crespo Gómez, Luis Colina, Stefano Carniani, Sarah Kendrew, Edoardo Iani, Angela Adamo, Abdurro'uf, Marianna Annunziatella, Stacey Alberts, Leindert A. Boogaard, Karina I. Caputi, Marco Castellano, Michele Catone, Rui Marques-Chaves, Ryan Cooper, Seiji Fujimoto, Mahmoud Hamed, Yuichi Harikane, Santosh Harish, Takuya Hashimoto, Jakob M. Helton, Tiger Y.-Y. Hsiao, Vasily Kokorev, Álvaro Labiano, Jens Melinder, Ikki Mitsuhashi, Göran Östlin, Lorenzo Napolitano, Borja Pérez-Díaz, Pablo G. Pérez-González, Carlota Prieto Jiménez, Giulia Rodighiero, Paola Santini, Ana Varo-O'Ferrall, Jorge A. Zavala, Yongda Zhu
abstract: Detailed UV-to-optical studies of galaxies at z >= 10 have largely focused on bright systems (MUV <= -20 mag), leaving intrinsically faint galaxies virtually unexplored to date. Combining NIRCam, NIRSpec, and MIRI imaging and spectroscopy, we investigate UNCOVER-ABELL2744-13151 (U13151), an ultra-faint galaxy at z = 9.7995 (MUV = -17.44 mag), magnified by Abell 2744 ($\mu$ = 12.8). U13151 is very blue ($\beta$ ~ -2.64), ultra-low mass (log10(M*/Msun) ~ 6.68), young (~ 5.5 Myr), metal-poor (Z ~ 3-6% Zsun), and compact (Re ~ 122 pc). It exhibits negligible dust attenuation, extreme ionization conditions, and intense star formation (sSFR(Ha) ~ 94 Gyr-1, or equivalently M*/SFR(Ha) ~ 10.6 Myr). Despite similarities with much brighter galaxies, its low C/O, approximately solar Ne/O, and undetected nitrogen emission suggest enrichment dominated by core-collapse supernovae, in stark contrast with similar nitrogen-enhanced systems. U13151 might be undergoing its first major episode of star formation, assembling most (if not all) of its M* through five unresolved clumps. Its high ionizing photon production efficiency (log10($\xi_{\rm ion}$/ (Hz erg-1)) ~ 25.64) suggests, through a simple toy model, suggests, through a simple toy model, that similarly short-lived episodes could contribute significantly to the ionizing photon budget of low-mass galaxies during Cosmic Reionization. We explore different evolutionary scenarios, from U13151-like galaxies potentially representing the progenitors of Blue Monsters at higher redshifts to the possibility that such systems could be the early building blocks of present-day Milky Way-like galaxies. Our results highlight the fundamental role of MIRI in studying galaxies in the early Universe and the urgent need to investigate the faintest, lowest-mass systems to shed light on the fundamental physics driving the earliest phases of galaxy formation.

title: Probing the Assembly of Triangulum: Precision Metallicities and $α$ Abundances of M33's Star Clusters from APOGEE Integrated-Light Spectroscopy
authors: Benjamin J. Gibson, Borja Anguiano, Sten Hasselquist, Gail Zasowski, Anil Seth, Rachael L. Beaton, Christian R. Hayes, Geraint F. Lewis, Steven R. Majewski, Giulia Pagnini
abstract: The star cluster system of M33 provides an excellent opportunity to investigate whether galaxy formation physics is dependent on a galaxy's mass. Older globular clusters (GCs) trace hierarchical assembly and chemical enrichment, while younger clusters trace the recent star formation. By studying the M33 star cluster system as a whole, we can probe the formation physics of galaxies at a lower mass than the Milky Way, and look for signals of accretion. To that end, we present analysis of 37 M33 star clusters using high-resolution ($R\sim22,500$), near-infrared (1.5-1.7 $\mu$m), integrated light spectra from the APOGEE survey. We use full-spectrum fitting to obtain precision measurements of the clusters' kinematics, metallicities, and $\alpha$ abundances. We identify three populations of clusters from our measurements: young stellar clusters (~100 Myr) with broad Brackett absorption features; intermediate-age clusters (1-2 Gyr) that are metal-rich ([M/H]=-0.5 to +0.3) with roughly solar $\alpha$ abundance; and old (>5 Gyr), kinematically-hot and metal-poor GCs. These old GCs exhibit a broad range of kinematics (RV~-250 to -8 km s$^{-1}$), metallicities ([M/H]=-1.8 to -0.6) and $\alpha$ abundances ([$\alpha$/M]=+0.05 to +0.3), and we identify and discuss three GCs that show strong chemodynamical evidence of accretion into M33's halo. M33's GCs at [M/H]~-1.2 have a spread in [$\alpha$/M] of nearly 0.2 dex. This pattern is strikingly similar to the abundance distribution of Milky Way GCs, and indicates either that M33 and the Milky Way formed clusters similarly at early times, or that M33 hosts a significant population of accreted clusters in its halo.

title: Extending the M33 Extinction Map with Radio and Far-Infrared Gas Observations
authors: Yuxi Wang
abstract: As the third-largest galaxy in the Local Group, M33 requires high-precision, wide-area extinction maps to recover the intrinsic luminosity and enable accurate studies, yet the available maps remain limited in coverage. In this work, we extend the stellar-based extinction map within the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury: Triangulum Extended Region (PHATTER) footprint to the outer disk by calibrating empirical $A_V$-H\,\textsc{i} and $A_V$-total hydrogen relations in the PHATTER overlap region. Within the PHATTER footprint, we retain the stellar-based map at 6$^{\prime\prime}$ resolution, and outside the area covered by the stellar-based extinction map we produce an extended map at $\approx 12^{\prime\prime}$ resolution. The resulting map preserves a continuous morphology across the PHATTER boundary and reveals clear spiral-arm and interarm contrast and patchy dust substructures across a broader area. The median and maximum extinction values, $\mathrm{median}(A_V)\approx 0.91$ mag and $A_{V,\mathrm{max}} \approx 2.62$ mag, are consistent with the high-extinction range reported by previous M33 studies, while naturally reflecting differences in tracers and spatial coverage. The extinction map provides a practical, publicly available dataset for galaxy-wide extinction correction and for further studies in M33.

title: The EMA Justitia Probe: Terminator Frame-Based Deployment Orbit Selection and Surface Coverage Analysis
authors: Shamil Biktimirov, Fatima Alnaqbi, Anton Ivanov
abstract: The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA) probe is designed to perform asteroid imaging during an uncontrolled ballistic descent to (269) Justitia. The mission design is constrained by main spacecraft proximity operations, uncertain asteroid gravity, limited knowledge of the final deployment trajectory, and requirements for illumination and safe operations. These constraints necessitate a mission design that ensures suitable illumination, attitude determination and control, and payload pointing throughout descent. The EMA probe concept of operations employs near-terminator deployment orbit geometry with continuous Sun visibility and two attitude control modes: single-axis Sun-spin for periodic imaging opportunities and three-axis asteroid-pointing for continuous asteroid visibility. Based on these modes, formal requirements are derived for deployment orbits that enable asteroid observations during ballistic descent. A deployment orbit selection method is developed using the terminator reference frame and a minimum boresight deviation margin. The method identifies families of orbit orientations satisfying illumination and payload observation constraints. Reference orbits are selected and verified through mission geometry analysis and trajectory propagation using a polyhedron gravity model. Asteroid surface coverage is then evaluated for uncontrolled tumbling, Sun-spin, and asteroid-pointing modes. The results characterize the expected imaging performance and demonstrate the feasibility of the EMA probe concept for close-proximity asteroid imaging. The proposed approach can also support future ballistic probe missions subject to similar operational and observational constraints.

title: ERGO-ML and how to directly infer the multi-temperature nature of intra-cluster gas: simulation-based inference with TNG-Cluster
authors: Joey Braspenning, Annalisa Pillepich, Marine Prunier, Dimitris Chatzigiannakis, Dylan Nelson
abstract: Though galaxy clusters are virialized and mostly in thermodynamic equilibrium, their internal gas thermodynamics are complex. The hot gas is multiphase and spatially inhomogeneous. The exact state of the gas contains important information about the internal physics governing clusters, however, measuring the multiphase distribution of the X-ray emitting gas is hard if not impossible with current observational methods. In this work (part of the ERGO-ML series), we present a direct inference method of the multiphase temperature distribution of the gas in the intra-cluster medium (ICM), applicable over a large range of spatial and mass scales. It works using different spectral resolutions (XRISM-like and Chandra-like) and realistic photon noise. Our method is an application of simulation-based inference. We train a neural-network on X-ray spectra in the range 0.1-10 keV, generated for $\approx 10^5$ sightlines of massive clusters ($M_{\rm 200c} = 10^{14.2-15.2}~\mathrm{M_\odot}$) from the TNG-Cluster cosmological MHD galaxy simulation. We show that our method recovers the mass-weighted temperature of both individual sightlines and entire clusters with an average prediction error of $< 0.01 ~\mathrm{dex}$, and the total gas mass within $0.04 ~\mathrm{dex}$. On top of that it gives accurate measures of the fraction of sub- and super-virial gas. Our method is capable of extracting the cooler gas phase even if the flux contribution is 3 orders of magnitude below that of the virial gas phase. We then show that we can accurately recover the spatial distribution of multi-phase gas both in relaxed and merging systems. This opens the way to studies of the multiphase nature of the ICM and the violent physics of feedback, accretion and merging.
comments: 21 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to MNRAS

figs.cap: Performance of the neural network for predicting gas masses for each of the five temperature bins, and the total gas mass along all sightlines in TNG-Cluster. All results are for the test set (93,600 sightlines). Left to right the first 5 columns show the performance in the temperature bins, the right-most column show the predicted total gas mass for each sightline. Lighter colours indicate more sightlines, contours show the levels where 25%, 50% and 75% of the sightlines included. The bottom row shows the ratio between the predicted and true gas masses. The one-to-one perfect prediction is indicated by the black dashed line. The numbers in the bottom-right corner indicate the fraction of sightlines with zero true gas mass in each temperature bin. A typical sightline has very good predictions between $10^{7}$ - $10^{8}~\mathrm{K}$, has a larger scatter, but no overall bias, for temperatures just cooler that that, but has large errors and biases for both the coldest and hottest gas. Looking at the gas mass distributions in the top panels this makes sense, as those temperatures are under-abundant by on average 2-3 orders of magnitude, hence contribute very little to the overall spectrum.

Cross-check of neural network performance against best-neighbours (top) and contribution to the input signal (bottom). The top panels show the five temperature bins (colours) and the gas mass (grey) prediction errors in normalised units. This is the MAE of the neural-network, the black line histogram is the MAE distribution of neighbours with a fixed distance, where the distance is chosen such that the KS-test statistic between the two distributions is minimized. Sightlines with zero prediction error, or zero difference between neighbours are shown as bars on the left-hand side, with the numbers indicating the fraction. These sightlines almost always have no gas in that particular temperature bin, rather than perfectly predicting the non-zero amount of gas. This allows to measure what the average difference in the spectrum is our model can resolve. The value $\bar{\Delta}$ gives the average fractional difference between the two neighbour spectra. We see that even for the worst performing temperature bin, our network can disentangle the underlying temperature distribution of spectra that differ on average by one part in a thousand. The bottom panels show the log absolute error (in dex) for each temperature bin, as a function of the fraction that the gas at that temperature contributes to the total spectrum. From left to right, the panels show the low-, mid-, and high-energy parts of the spectrum, where different temperatures are expected to dominate. Only non-zero predictions are shown, this mostly affects the highest temperature bins, where only 17% of all sightlines have non-zero values (see top figure).

Performance of our method at the map-wide, cluster level. Here we show gas temperature maps for 5 example clusters from the test set showing a diverse range of morphologies. The top rows show the predicted gas mass maps in the 5 temperature bins, the bottom rows show the ground truth. The intensity of the colour encodes the relative abundance of a temperature along each sightline. The red boxes enclose temperatures that harbour at least 10 per cent of the total gas mass of the cluster. The gas fraction in each temperature bin is listed in the top left corners, and the halo mass in the bottom right corner of each set of panels for the clusters. Both more relaxed objects, and merger morphologies are well reproduced.

Temperature distributions and predictions for an example $M_{\rm 500c}=10^{15}~\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$ cluster, showing the summed result for the full $R_{\rm 500c}$ region (316 sightlines) on top, the core region ($<0.2~R_{\rm 500c}$, 12 sightlines) in the middle, and massive satellites in the outskirts ($M_{\star}>10^{11}~\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$; $r>0.5~R_{\rm 500c}$, 12 sightlines) in the bottom panels. Black horizontal lines indicate the true gas mass in each bin, coloured bars indicate the predicted gas mass in the same bin. Right panels show the total spectrum in black: this is the only input to the neural network. Coloured spectra show, for each temperature bin in the left panel, the corresponding spectrum (which the network never sees). This shows that the cooler gas is sub-dominant in the total spectrum by multiple orders of magnitude. Nevertheless, we can still accurately predict the gas mass, likely due to the subtle changes in individual emission lines.

Performance of our method on the sub-virial gas profiles. Median surface density profiles of virial temperature gas (red), and sub-virial gas (blue) in 3 halo mass bins. Solid lines and shaded regions show the inference from with our model, and halo-to-halo variation. Dashed lines show the true profiles, both are measured from the pixelated maps. Both the virial gas and the cooler gas profile are recovered excellently at all halo masses. The virial gas follows the halo density profile, decreasing monotonically with radius, whereas the cooler gas has a near constant surface density within $R_{\rm 500c}$.

Feature importance of the input X-ray spectra for the prediction of different temperatures. Red and blue colours respectively indicate the top 5% positive and negative SHAP values for predicting the gas mass in each temperature bin. A positive value (red) indicates that a larger flux at that energy boosts the prediction, while for a negative value (blue) a larger flux would suppress the prediction. We note that there are two regions of primary interest to the network: the first is low energies ($E<1~\mathrm{keV}$), the second at high energies ($6~\mathrm{keV}<E<8~\mathrm{keV}$), with other regions of the spectrum contributing little information. Two example spectra for a cool sightline (blue) and hot sightline (red) are shown on top.

title: Evolving only the observed spacetime region: perfectly parallel lightcone simulations with sCOLA
authors: Mayeul Aubin, Florent Leclercq, Guilhem Lavaux
abstract: Cosmological analyses of Stage-IV galaxy surveys require large ensembles of lightcone mock catalogues, but a full survey-scale $N$-body run costs of order $10^7$ CPU hours, putting such ensembles out of reach. We present a framework that produces survey-scale dark matter lightcones for a typical cost of order $10^3$ CPU hours each, based on the spatial COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (sCOLA) method. sCOLA decomposes an arbitrarily large volume into small tiles that are evolved independently, with buffer regions and non-periodic boundary conditions on the gravitational potential. We combine it with on-the-fly lightcone building, so that the evolved spacetime region reduces to the observed one: each tile is stopped as soon as the observer's past lightcone has left it, and only the tiles intersecting the region of interest are simulated at all. We further introduce two accuracy improvements to the sCOLA formalism: an LPT buffer that approximates the inflow of particles from outside the sCOLA box, and a second-order perturbative approximation to the gravitational potential at its boundaries; together they remove the large-scale inaccuracies of previous work and allow smaller tiles and buffers. Against a \texttt{Gadget4} reference in a $3.84\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc}$ box with $3\,840^3$ particles, up to $k \simeq 0.4\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ the sCOLA lightcone reproduces the matter power spectrum to 1%, the velocity divergence power spectrum to 1.5% and the equilateral bispectrum to 2%, with no visible discontinuity at tile boundaries. The run cost $1\,300$ CPU hours, a factor of $2\,600$ below our $\texttt{Gadget4}$ run. Perfect parallelism at this cost brings ensembles of thousands of survey-scale lightcones within reach of a single allocation: $\sim 25\,000$ realisations of the $\textit{Euclid}$ Galactic north cap with a mass resolution of $10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ for $10^{7}$ CPU hours.

figs.cap: Illustration of sCOLA with an LPT buffer: an arbitrarily large volume is split into small tiles that are simulated independently. Particles are represented as vertices of the Lagrangian grid. The LPT buffer (new in this work, in blue) approximates the inflow of particles from outside the sCOLA box (defined as the tile in white, plus its buffer in orange) as the Lagrangian grid deforms. Non-periodic boundary conditions on the gravitational potential $\Phi$ (improved in this work) account for the large-scale gravitational field in which the sCOLA box is embedded.

sCOLA lightcone building: each tile is evolved only until the lightcone has left it, reducing the number of required time steps. Tiles farther from the observer are crossed by the lightcone earlier and require fewer time steps.

Mean number of time steps needed to build a lightcone with sCOLA, $\langle n_{\mathrm{steps}}\rangle$ (averaged over sCOLA boxes), divided by the number of time steps $n_{\mathrm{steps}}$ needed to evolve each sCOLA box to $a_{0}=1$, as a function of the size of the full box. We distinguish the cases of a cubical octant (the full volume is evolved) and a spherical octant (only the tiles in the sphere are evolved). We compare the ideal case of arbitrarily small tiles and an infinite number of time steps (dashed lines) to the realistic configuration used in this work, i.e. ten time steps and tiles of size $64\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ (solid lines). For the $3.84\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc}$ cubical octant of this work, building the lightcone with sCOLA requires 57% fewer time steps than evolving the full volume to $a_{0}=1$.

Slice of the Main simulation lightcone dark matter density field for Gadget4 (top row) and sCOLA (middle row), shown as $\log_{10}(2+\delta)$. The bottom row displays the difference in $\log_{10}(2+\delta)$ between the two fields, with the sCOLA tiling represented as dashed lines. The observer is located at $(0,0)$ (bottom left corner), coordinates are in $h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, and the full box is a cube of side $3.84\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc}$. sCOLA reproduces the Gadget4 density field with no visible tile-boundary artefacts, with a mean absolute difference in $\log_{10}(2+\delta)$ of $0.036$.

Slice of the Main simulation lightcone velocity field for Gadget4 (top row) and sCOLA (middle row). We plot the line-of-sight velocity component $v_{\parallel}$ in $\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The bottom row displays the difference between the two velocity fields, with the sCOLA tiling represented as dashed lines. sCOLA reproduces the Gadget4 velocity field with only a handful of visible tile-boundary artefacts; the mean absolute difference in $v_{\parallel}$ is $9.67\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

Comparison of the matter density power spectrum and cross-correlations between Gadget4, sCOLA and tCOLA on the Mini and Main lightcone simulations, for 10 and 100 time steps ($n_{\mathrm{steps}}$ variable). For the power spectrum, we plot the ratio to the reference Gadget4 power spectrum. The grey bands are 1% and 2% around Gadget4. The cross-correlations are also computed with respect to Gadget4; there, the grey bands are 1‰ and 2‰. sCOLA reaches 1% agreement with Gadget4 up to $k\simeq 0.4\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ with 10 time steps; the residual bump near the sCOLA box scale stays within 1%. The fundamental modes of the tile and the sCOLA box are denoted $k_{\mathrm{tile}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{sCOLA}}$, respectively.

title: Neutrino self-interactions in light of DESI and CMB-SPA
authors: Hernán E. Noriega, Josue De-Santiago, Gabriela Garcia-Arroyo, Ivan Pérez-Castro, Jorge Venzor
abstract:
We present an updated analysis of non-standard neutrino self-interactions, where the interaction is effectively mediated by a heavy particle, using the latest available data from DESI and the CMB. The considered data include combinations of DESI DR1 full-shape galaxy clustering (FS), BAO distance measurements, Lyman-$\alpha$ 1D power spectra (Ly-$\alpha$), and a combined CMB likelihood (CMB-SPA) using data from Planck, ACT, and SPT. First, we probe two DESI DR1-only datasets, where the effective interaction parameter $G_{m eff}$ is multimodal in the profile likelihood, leading us to analyze two different regimes: moderately interacting (MI$_
u$) and strongly interacting (SI$_
u$) neutrinos. With FS+BAO, the evidence disfavors the SI$_
u$ mode, a trend that becomes slightly stronger with the inclusion of Ly-$\alpha$. However, in the latter dataset, the MI$_
u$ region shows a bimodality in which the intermediate mode is very sharp and peaks around $G_{m eff\,} \simeq 10^{-3} \mathrm{MeV}^{-2}$; interestingly, this mode is not penalized versus the weaker standard-like mode. Furthermore, we test CMB and DESI joint data and show that the SI$_
u$ mode is more disfavored by CMB-SPA than by Planck-only data. In particular, the evidence against this mode becomes the strongest thus far (with odds of 5:100000) in the FS+BAO+CMB-SPA combination.
comments: 20 pages, 10 figures

figs.cap: Profile likelihood (normalized to $\Lambda$CDM) of the NSI parameter $\log_{10}(G_{\rm eff\,}{\rm MeV^{2}})$, obtained from the analyses of DESI DR1 (FS+BAO)+BBN+$n_{s10}$ (blue) and DESI DR1 (FS+BAO+Ly-$\alpha$)+BBN+$n_{s10}$ (red). Here, we kept the total neutrino mass and effective number of relativistic species fixed at $\sum m_{\nu}=0.06\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $N_{\rm eff}=3.046$.

Posterior distributions at 68% and 95% CLs on the cosmological parameters of the NSI model with fixed neutrino mass, considering DESI DR1 (FS+BAO)+BBN+$n_{s10}$ (left), and including Ly-$\alpha$ data (right). For comparison, we also show the $\Lambda$CDM bounds (gray) on the left. The corresponding parameter constraints are reported in Table 2. The full contour plot for the FS+BAO case, including a comparison with free neutrino mass, is shown in Fig. 8.

Comparison of the one-dimensional marginalized posteriors of $\log_{10}(G_{\rm eff\,}{\rm MeV^{2}})$ obtained from DESI DR1 (FS+BAO)+BBN+$n_{s10}$ (blue) and from the same dataset including Ly-$\alpha$ data (red). The latter shifts the posteriors toward larger values of the neutrino self-interaction coupling.

Posterior distributions at 68% and 95% CLs on the cosmological parameters of the NSI model with fixed neutrino mass, considering DESI DR2 BAO+CMB-SPA. For comparison, we also show the $\Lambda$CDM bounds (gray). The corresponding parameter constraints are reported in Table 3. The full contour plot, including a comparison with free $\sum m_{\nu}$ and $N_{\rm eff}$, is shown in Fig. 9.

One-dimensional marginalized posterior distributions for $\log_{10}(G_{\rm eff\,}{\rm MeV^{2}})$ (left) and $\sum m_{\nu}$ (right), obtained by fitting the NSI model to the DESI DR2 BAO+CMB-SPA data. Solid curves represent the moderate mode, while dashed curves correspond to the strong mode.

1-D posterior distributions of $\log_{10}(G_{\rm eff}\,{\rm MeV}^{2})$ obtained from DESI DR1 (FS+BAO)+CMB-SPA, each normalized to its maximum. The blue solid and dashed curves show the moderately interacting and strongly interacting regimes, respectively. The black dash-dotted curve shows the posterior obtained by extending the lower bound of the prior for the strongly interacting regime from $-2.0$ to $-2.5$. The posterior maximum follows the lower prior boundary, indicating that the apparent peak at $\log_{10}(G_{\rm eff}\,{\rm MeV}^{2})=-2.0$ is a boundary effect. Cosmological constraints are reported in Table 3, while the full contour plot is presented in Fig. 10.

title: Detection Forecasting for Blazars at MeV Energies with Fermi-LAT Swift-BAT Cross Match
authors: Timothy Wessling-Resnick, Naomi Tsuji, Tsuguo Aramaki, Paolo Coppi, Manel Errando, Yoshiyuki Inoue, Reshmi Mukherjee, Svanik Tandon, Jiancheng Zeng
abstract: Over the past two decades, the lack of an MeV $\gamma$-ray all-sky instrument has left an observational gap in blazar broadband emission. Recently, a new suite of MeV $\gamma$-ray instruments with sensitivity in the $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-12}$ $\mathrm{erg/cm^{2}/s}$ range has been proposed, with the potential to far surpass the capabilities of previous all-sky MeV instruments. In this work, we forecast the capabilities of future MeV $\gamma$-ray instruments including COSI, GRAMS, newASTROGAM, and AMEGO-X to observe blazars. We pair total source count estimates of blazar luminosity functions with SED-modeled flux estimates of 76 blazars selected from a sample of 115 blazars cross-matched between the latest Fermi-LAT and Swift-BAT catalogs. We forecast that an instrument with a sensitivity limit of $10^{-11}$ $\mathrm{erg/cm^{2}/s}$ could detect 61 of the 76 SED-modeled blazars, and expect a total population of a few tens to a few hundreds of Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSRQs), as well as a few hundred BL Lacs (BLLs). An instrument with a sensitivity limit of $10^{-12}$ $\mathrm{erg/cm^{2}/s}$ could detect all 76 of the SED-modeled blazars, and we expect a total population of a few hundred to one thousand FSRQs and roughly one thousand BLLs. As MeV blazars have been observed to be extremely luminous and MeV $\gamma$-rays are minimally attenuated by the extragalactic background light, we use luminosity functions to estimate that blazars could be detected out to $z\approx6$. Lastly, we demonstrate detectability for blazars that have been proposed as neutrino-emitting candidates, as the MeV regime could provide a window into resolving lepto-hadronic degeneracies.
comments: Initial Arxiv submission. 25 pages, 7 figures

title: Mean-Field Backreaction in Single-Field Inflation
authors: Matteo Braglia, Gabriele Franciolini, Nadir Ijaz, Marco Peloso
abstract: The validity of linear perturbation theory and the role of backreaction in single-field inflationary models that enhance power at small scales have recently been under debate. We investigate scalar backreaction semi-analytically in a mean-field approach within the decoupling limit, considering popular models with a transient ultra-slow-roll (USR) stage or an oscillatory feature (OF) in the potential. We find that ultraviolet (UV) modes in the Bunch--Davies vacuum can substantially affect backreaction estimates unless removed by adiabatic subtraction. Our mean-field treatment can reproduce recent lattice results, but reveals a spurious sensitivity to UV contributions in some cases. This sensitivity is reduced in the OF model when copious particle production separates the amplified physical modes from the UV vacuum tail, making lattice results more reliable in this regime. In USR, instead, adiabatically subtracted spectra yield milder backreaction on the background evolution than previously inferred.
comments: 47 pages, 11 figures

figs.cap: The two benchmark models used in our analysis: USR (left) and OF (right). Upper panels show the potential $V[\varphi(N)]/V_{0}$ along each (non-backreacted) background trajectory. Both horizontal axes show $N-N_{\rm in}$, measured from the onset of the respective feature. For OF, $N_{\rm in}$ corresponds to $\varphi=\varphi_{0}$, while $\varphi_{s}$ marks the end of the feature. The two vertical lines in the upper-right panel mark these field crossings. Both panels display $V/V_{0}$, with a finer vertical scale in the OF panel to resolve its small variations. Lower panels show $\epsilon_{H}$ and $|\eta_{H}|$; the $\eta_{H}$ curve is solid where $\eta_{H}>0$ and dashed where $\eta_{H}<0$. The shaded band marks the OF interval. USR has a single smooth episode in which $|\eta_{H}|$ reaches a few and $\epsilon_{H}$ falls exponentially. The OF benchmark model instead has a short burst of rapid oscillations reaching $|\eta_{H}|\sim 6$, while $\epsilon_{H}$ remains of order $10^{-6}$.
